findings.title: Upload permission check cannot run before Multer buffers the body, and nginx lifts the body limit for every /v1 route
findings.section: 2. Upload, processing and access control / 3. Serving and caching
findings.problem: The spec lists 'Permission products.media' as check 1 and Multer as check 2. The existing admin code does not use a guard: each handler calls this.auth.staff(authorization) then this.require(role, perm) inside the service method. A Nest FileInterceptor runs before the handler, so Multer would buffer up to 10 MB in memory for any caller, including unauthenticated or Operations/CS callers, before the 403 is produced. Separately, client_max_body_size 11m is set on all of location /v1/, so login, webhook and every other public route accept 11 MB bodies at the proxy. This breaks least privilege (constraint 6) and is a cheap memory-exhaustion path on the API container that also serves checkout.
findings.evidence: spec: 'Checks on upload, in order. 1. Permission products.media ... 2. Multer in-memory' and '`client_max_body_size 11m;` on `location /v1/`'. server/src/commerce/admin.service.ts:113-115 `const user = await this.auth.staff(authorization); this.require(user.role, "customers.contact.reveal");` (check done inside the handler, not a guard). web/nginx.conf:16 `location /v1/ {`.
findings.fix:
Section 2, replace check 1 and 2 text with: "1. Before any body is read: authentication and the `products.media` permission run in a Nest guard (or path-scoped middleware) that executes before the Multer interceptor, reusing `auth.staff()` and the RBAC matrix. A request with no valid staff session is answered 401, one without the permission 403, and in both cases the body is never read into memory. The product-exists check (404) runs in the handler after Multer, because it needs no body but may share the handler. 2. Multer in-memory with `limits: { files: 1, fields: 2, parts: 4, fileSize: 10 MB }`; exceeding fileSize returns 413 TOO_LARGE." Add a test: "A 10 MB multipart body with no cookie returns 401, and with an Operations cookie returns 403, and in both cases the Multer interceptor never ran (assert with a spy or by checking no buffer was allocated)."

Section 3, replace the `client_max_body_size 11m;` bullet with: "`location /v1/` keeps nginx's default `client_max_body_size` of 1 MB. A second location, `location ~ ^/v1/admin/products/[^/]+/images$`, sets `client_max_body_size 11m;` and repeats the same `proxy_pass http://api:8080;`, `proxy_http_version 1.1;`, `Host` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` lines as `location /v1/` (a regex location does not inherit them), and `limit_except POST { deny all; }`. nginx answers a body above its limit with an HTML 413 page, so the admin client maps any 413 response, JSON or not, to the TOO_LARGE message." Add a test or deploy check: "POST a 2 MB body to /v1/auth/login through nginx returns 413; the same size to the image upload path reaches the API."
findings.verifyReason: Both halves check out. (1) The spec's "Checks on upload" list puts Permission products.media at step 1 and Multer in-memory at step 2. Every existing admin handler authenticates inside the service method (`await this.auth.staff(authorization)` then `this.require(role, perm)`, e.g. admin.service.ts lines 25-26 and 41-42), and there is no Nest guard pattern for admin routes. A FileInterceptor runs before the handler, so Multer would buffer up to 10 MB for unauthenticated or Operations/CS callers before the 403. The order in the spec cannot hold with the planned wiring. (2) web/nginx.conf currently has a single `location /v1/` that proxies everything to the API. The spec adds `client_max_body_size 11m;` on that location, so login, webhook, checkout and every other public route would accept 11 MB bodies. This conflicts with RBAC least privilege (constraint 6) and puts memory pressure on the same API container that serves checkout. The fix does not reverse any owner decision. It only adds an ordering constraint and narrows the body limit. One refinement: nginx cannot pick a location by a regex that spans `/v1/` and the exact upload path unless the regex location is declared and carries its own proxy_pass, so the spec must say the regex location repeats the proxy settings.

findings.title: Cleaning up content-addressed files can delete files that a live photo row still uses
findings.section: 2. Upload, processing and access control (Order of work)
findings.problem: Names are {productId}/{hash16}-{width}.webp, so two requests for the same photo on the same product write the SAME three keys. If the second upload fails on unique(productId,hash) (duplicate) or on the position key, 'delete the files again' removes the keys the first, committed row points to, and every cached link 404s while the shop shows a broken photo (then the drawing). The same collision exists after Delete (files removed after commit) racing with a re-upload of the same photo: the new row commits, its files are gone. The spec also never says when the duplicate check runs (before writing, or only via the unique key at commit).
findings.evidence: spec L55 `media/products/{productId}/{hash16}-{width}.webp`; L101 'same photo uploaded twice ... refused'; L105 'if the transaction fails, delete the files again'; L107 'then delete the files'.
findings.fix:
Replace the Upload and Delete bullets in "Order of work" (L105 and L107) with the two bullets below. Add one sentence to L101: "The duplicate check runs under the product lock, before any file is written."

- Upload: process the photo in memory first, with no lock and no writes. Then open one transaction and take the product lock as its first statement (`SELECT id FROM "Product" WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE`). Under the lock, in this order: (1) if a row with the same `(productId, hash)` exists, answer 409 "Foto ini sudah ada di produk ini" and write nothing; (2) if the product already has 6 photos, refuse; (3) pick the first free position; (4) PUT the three WebP files; (5) insert the row and the audit entry; (6) commit. If anything fails after the first PUT, delete only the keys this request wrote. Because step (1) found no row with this hash, those keys are not used by any row of the same product. Never delete a key that a row of the same product references. The `(productId, position)` unique key stays as a second safety net and still returns 409 "Foto lain sedang diunggah. Coba lagi." if it fires.

- Delete: open one transaction and take the same product lock first. Delete the row (variant links clear through `onDelete: SetNull`), close the gap in positions and write the audit entry. Still inside the transaction, delete the three files, but only if no other row of the same product has the same hash (the unique key makes that case impossible today, so keep the check as a guard). Then commit. A failed file delete is logged and only leaves an unlinked file. Because a re-upload of the same photo must wait for the lock, it can no longer commit a row whose files a concurrent delete then removes. Reorder takes the same product lock.

Add to the test list at L185: "same photo uploaded twice at once keeps the first row's files; delete followed immediately by re-upload of the same photo leaves the files in place."
findings.verifyReason: Spec L55 names files {productId}/{hash16}-{width}.webp, so the same photo on the same product always maps to the same three keys. L105 writes the files first, then runs the transaction, and on failure deletes the files again. L101 says a duplicate is refused but never says when the check runs, so it can only be the unique(productId,hash) key at commit, after the PUTs. Failure scenario: upload A commits. A second upload of the same photo (or a concurrent one) overwrites the same keys, fails on the unique key, and its cleanup deletes the keys that A's committed row points to. The shop then serves 404s for a live photo. L107 deletes files after commit, so a delete racing with a re-upload of the same photo removes the new row's files in the same way. The fix keeps the content-addressed names and the 6-photo, audit and 409 decisions, so it does not reverse any approved owner decision. The reviewer's fix cites "the next finding" for the lock. The refined text below is self-contained. It also keeps the existing "Foto lain sedang diunggah" 409 as a fallback.

findings.title: Concurrency tests (two uploads, delete vs reorder) cannot be written against the existing fake-db, and a P2002 unique violation has no error mapping
findings.section: Testing / 2. Upload, processing and access control (Order of work)
findings.problem: The spec's only protection against a seventh photo and a position collision is the DB unique key (productId, position) turned into 409. src/test/fake-db.ts serialises every $transaction on a promise chain and models no unique constraints, no cascade and no productImage table, so two simultaneous uploads simply run one after the other and both succeed (or both read the same count). The test 'two simultaneous uploads (fake database like src/test/fake-db.ts)' therefore passes or fails for the wrong reason. The +100 reorder trick is likewise untestable without a fake that enforces uniqueness. Separately, ApiExceptionFilter only maps P2028/P2034; a Prisma P2002 would fall through to the generic path, so the promised 409 'Foto lain sedang diunggah' does not exist yet and is not covered by any listed test.
findings.evidence: server/src/test/fake-db.ts:11-12 'Transactions run one at a time (like row locks on one order)'; tx has no productImage. server/src/api-exception.filter.ts:5 'BUSY_CODES = new Set(["P2028", "P2034"])'. Spec: 'the (productId, position) unique key makes the second fail with 409'.
findings.fix:
In Testing, replace the bullet "Six-photo limit, duplicate photo, two simultaneous uploads (fake database like `src/test/fake-db.ts`), reorder with a stale list, delete clearing a variant link." with:

"Media tests use a new in-memory fake, `src/test/fake-media-db.ts` (the existing `src/test/fake-db.ts` models only orders and stock and serialises transactions, so it cannot show a unique-key race). It has `productImage` and `variant` tables. It does NOT serialise transactions: each transaction works on a snapshot of its own writes and is applied on commit. It enforces the unique keys (productId, position) and (productId, hash) at write time by throwing `new Prisma.PrismaClientKnownRequestError(..., { code: 'P2002', meta: { target: [...] } })`. A transaction that throws is rolled back. It implements `variant.imageId` SetNull on image delete. A test hook (a gate promise) can pause a transaction after it has read the count and free position and before it inserts. A fake storage records put and delete calls.
- Two simultaneous uploads: start both service calls with `Promise.all`, hold both at the gate until both have read, then release. Assert exactly one 201 and one 409 `CONFLICT` "Foto lain sedang diunggah. Coba lagi.", exactly one row at that position, and that the loser's files were deleted from the fake storage (0 stray files).
- Reorder: with the +100 shift, the unique key never collides mid-way, and a stale id list gives 409 "Urutan foto berubah. Muat ulang halaman."
- Also cover the six-photo limit, a duplicate photo, and delete clearing a variant link.
Error mapping: `ApiExceptionFilter` (or the media service, which then rethrows an `HttpException`) maps a Prisma P2002 whose target includes `position` to 409 `CONFLICT` "Foto lain sedang diunggah. Coba lagi.", and one whose target includes `hash` to 409 `CONFLICT` "Foto ini sudah ada di produk ini." Any other P2002 keeps the generic path. One unit test per mapping.
The fake cannot prove real Postgres behaviour. Add one dev-server check that fires 2 parallel uploads at a product holding 5 photos and expects one 201 and one 409, and that the product ends with exactly 6 photos."
findings.verifyReason: Checked. Spec line 105 relies on the (productId, position) unique key to give a 409, and line 185 lists a "two simultaneous uploads (fake database like src/test/fake-db.ts)" test. The spec never mentions P2002 or its mapping, though the error table (lines 167-170) promises the 409s. server/src/test/fake-db.ts has no productImage or variant model and no unique constraints. Its $transaction serialises every call on a promise chain (lines 6-8, 12, 34-45), so two uploads would run one after the other. The second would see the first's row and hit the six-photo limit check or take the next position, so the unique-key path is never exercised. server/src/api-exception.filter.ts maps only P2028 and P2034 (line 6). A Prisma P2002 falls through to the generic path and returns 500 INTERNAL, so the promised 409 does not exist yet. The claim holds. One correction to the reviewer's fix: a gate placed inside the transaction would deadlock against the serial chain, and with the serial chain the second upload never reads a stale position. The media fake must therefore not serialise transactions. It should run each transaction on a snapshot and enforce uniqueness at write time, like Postgres READ COMMITTED. The gate sits between the read of the free position and the insert. This does not reverse any owner decision.

findings.title: Credit line under the gallery only does not satisfy CC BY / CC BY-SA attribution where the photo also appears on cards, cart and account
findings.section: 4. Storefront and admin screens (credit line) and 5. Demo photos, credits and removal
findings.problem: The spec shows credit only 'under the gallery' of the product page, and only for the current main photo. The same photo is shown as a card image, thumbnail, cart row and two account rows (ProductPhoto replaces ProductArt in all of them). CC BY 4.0 s.3(a) requires attribution for each use or sharing of the licensed material, in a manner reasonable to the medium, including creator, licence notice with a link to the licence, a link to the material, and an indication that it was modified. The proposed line 'Foto: {creator} · {licence}' links only to the source page, not the licence text, and does not say the photo was resized/converted/cropped. Thumbnails of photos 2 to 6 never get a credit while visible. For CC BY-SA the spec says copies 'carry the same licence' but nothing in the storefront or API states it. The API payload also drops licenceUrl, so the UI cannot link the licence.
findings.evidence: Spec line 133: 'Under the gallery, for a photo with `credit`: one line "Foto: {creator} · {licence}" ... linked to the source page.' Spec line 66: credit = { creator, licence, sourceUrl } (no licenceUrl). Spec line 131: ProductPhoto used in ProductCard, ProductPage, CartPage, Account (x2). Spec line 150: 'CC BY-SA only if nothing else fits (credit, and our resized copies carry the same licence)'.
findings.fix:
1) Section 1 JSON (line 66), replace the credit example with: "credit": { "creator": "…", "licence": "CC BY 4.0", "licenceUrl": "https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/", "sourceUrl": "https://…", "title": "…" }. Line 70: "credit is present only when creditRequired is true and carries licenceUrl and title."

2) Replace line 133 with: "Credit rule: every photo with credit is attributed in two places. (a) Under the gallery, one line for the photo currently shown, in the existing muted small text: 'Foto: {creator} · {licence} (diubah)', with the creator linked to sourceUrl and the licence linked to licenceUrl. It updates when a thumbnail or variant changes the main photo. (b) A public page /foto ('Kredit foto', linked from the footer on every page) listing per credited photo: title, creator, licence name linked to licenceUrl, source link, and the note 'Diubah ukurannya dan dikonversi ke WebP; dipotong persegi oleh bingkai.' Cards, cart and account rows show no inline credit; this is acceptable because the product-page line and /foto exist. Nothing is shown for credit-free licences. Add /v1/photo-credits (or reuse the catalogue) to cache-policy.ts as a public route."

3) Section 5, after line 150, add: "A CC BY-SA photo is marked 'CC BY-SA 4.0' on /foto with the note 'Salinan yang diubah ukurannya dibagikan dengan lisensi yang sama.' The owner approves any such photo in Appendix A knowing our resized copies are published under that licence. Because the sample set is removed before a client launch (line 143 banner), no share-alike obligation passes to the client fork."

4) Tests (near line 188): the catalogue returns licenceUrl for credited photos; /foto lists every creditRequired photo and none without credit; the product-page credit line changes with the selected thumbnail.

5) Mark this as an owner decision (new /foto page and footer link) in the owner approval list before implementation."
findings.verifyReason: The gaps are real, though "blocker" overstates it because the demo prefers credit-free licences and credit is conditional. The spec line 66 payload has creator, licence and sourceUrl but no licenceUrl, although the DB and samples.json store it (lines 46, 153). So the UI cannot link the licence text. Line 133 shows credit only under the gallery, for the shown photo. Thumbnails 2 to 6, cards, cart and account rows (line 131) show none. Nothing says the photo was resized, converted or cropped. Line 150 says CC BY-SA copies carry the same licence, but nothing in the storefront states it. CC BY 4.0 s.3(a) does allow attribution by a hyperlink to a resource carrying the required information, so a /foto page plus the product-page line is a legitimate reasonable-manner fix. It reverses no approved owner decision (CC BY credited, CC BY-SA last resort). A new public page is new scope, so it needs owner OK. The spec has no hint of the share-alike note.

findings.title: Stock/sample photos can be read by shoppers as the actual product, and nothing on the storefront says otherwise
findings.section: 5. Demo photos, credits and removal / Risks
findings.problem: The only mitigation for a sample photo being taken as the real product is an admin-only banner, a launch checklist item and a manual script. The storefront (the public dev IP serves a working checkout with prices) shows the photo with no indication that it is illustrative. Under Indonesian consumer protection law (UU 8/1999 art. 8 and 9, goods must match their description and presentation) a photo of a different item, shown on a priced and purchasable page, is a misrepresentation risk once any client forks the template and forgets the script. The decision to use samples is fixed, but the spec makes the safeguard depend entirely on humans remembering.
findings.evidence: Spec line 143 (banner only in admin photo manager), line 155 (checklist + script), line 211 'Sample photos left on a live client shop and read as the client's own product: sample tag, admin banner, launch checklist and the removal script.' Storefront section (lines 129-133) has no sample marker for shoppers.
findings.fix:
Section 4, Storefront, add after line 133: "A photo with `source: "sample"` shows the caption "Foto contoh" (existing muted small text, under the product page gallery, shown regardless of licence; if a credit line also applies, it reads "Foto contoh · Foto: {creator} · {licence}"). No badge on cards, cart or account rows. The catalogue response adds `sample: true` to such photos so the web app needs no extra request. The marker disappears when `remove-samples` runs or staff replace the photo."

Section 5, add after line 155: "The sample marker is shown to shoppers so the demo never presents a stock photo as the client's own product. LAUNCH_CHECKLIST 'Before launch' item: no `source: "sample"` photo remains on a live shop. Optional, owner to decide: add env var `SHOP_LIVE` (default false, documented in `.env.example`). When it is true, the API logs a warning with the count of sample rows at start, and `media:seed` refuses to run."

Testing section, add: (1) the catalogue marks sample photos `sample: true` and upload photos not; (2) `ProductPage` renders "Foto contoh" for a sample photo, including a CC0 one with no credit; (3) if the optional `SHOP_LIVE` guard is adopted, `media:seed` exits non-zero when it is true."
findings.verifyReason: The gap is real. Section 4 Storefront (lines 129-133) has no shopper-facing marker for sample photos. Line 133 shows a credit line only for licences that require credit, so a CC0 or Unsplash sample shows nothing at all. The only markers are admin-side (line 143 banner, line 155 checklist and script). The owner decision ("marked as samples to replace per client") is not reversed by a caption. The caption is the minimum fix. "Blocker" overstates it for the demo, but the risk is real once a client forks the template. The hard production-start refusal is heavier than needed and adds a new env var, so it should be an optional, owner-decided addition. The refusal could also block a client that intentionally keeps a licensed sample.

findings.title: Failed duplicate/racing upload deletes the files of the existing photo
findings.section: 2. Upload, processing and access control (Order of work, Upload)
findings.problem: File keys are content-addressed ({hash16}-{width}.webp) and the upload writes files to MinIO before the transaction. Uploading the same photo again, or two racing uploads of the same photo, writes to the same keys as the existing photo. When the transaction then fails on @@unique([productId, hash]), the spec says 'delete the files again', which removes the files the already-saved photo points to. Result: a live product photo that 404s. The spec only says the duplicate is refused; it does not say when the check runs or how it is told apart from the position collision (both are Prisma P2002 on different unique keys, mapped to different 409 messages).
findings.evidence: spec: 'media/products/{productId}/{hash16}-{width}.webp'; 'write the WebP files to MinIO; then in one transaction insert the row... if the transaction fails, delete the files again'; 'The same photo uploaded twice to one product is refused'
findings.fix:
In section 2, "Order of work", replace the Upload bullet (line 105) with:

"Upload: compute the hash of the largest processed copy, then look up (productId, hash). If a row exists, return 409 "Foto ini sudah ada di produk ini" before writing anything to MinIO. Otherwise write the WebP files, then in one transaction insert the row at the first free position and write the audit entry. Files are named by hash, so a failed upload must never delete files that a saved photo may use. If the transaction fails, re-read (productId, hash) and delete the files only when no ProductImage row with that hash exists for the product. If the re-read finds a row, or fails, leave the files in place; a leftover unlinked file is harmless, a deleted live photo is not. Map P2002 by inspecting meta.target: (productId, hash) gives 409 "Foto ini sudah ada di produk ini", and (productId, position) gives 409 "Foto lain sedang diunggah. Coba lagi." Two uploads at once on the same product still cannot create a seventh photo, because of the (productId, position) unique key."

Add to the test list (section 7 / unit tests): "A duplicate upload (same product, same hash) returns 409 and leaves the original files in storage. A failed transaction for a different hash deletes only its own files."
findings.verifyReason: Spec line 55 makes keys content-addressed (media/products/{productId}/{hash16}-{width}.webp), and line 101 says a duplicate is refused without saying when the check runs. Line 105 writes files to MinIO first, and says "if the transaction fails, delete the files again". A duplicate upload therefore writes to the same keys as the saved photo, fails on @@unique([productId, hash]), and the cleanup deletes the files the saved photo uses. That leaves a live photo that 404s. Line 105 also covers only the (productId, position) collision (409 "Foto lain sedang diunggah"). Both unique violations are Prisma P2002 on different targets, and the spec does not say how to tell them apart. The reviewer's fix is sound and does not reverse an owner decision. One small gap remains in it: a re-check after failure can still race with an in-flight identical upload, so the refinement below also lets a failed upload leave the files in place when it cannot be sure.

findings.title: Bucket policy is applied at start-up without replace-and-verify semantics or a failure rule, and the dev checks never prove other prefixes stay private
findings.problem: ObjectStorage today only does HeadBucket/CreateBucket. The spec adds an anonymous GetObject policy but does not say whether PutBucketPolicy replaces or merges with an existing policy, what happens if the API key lacks admin rights (crash loop vs silent skip), or how a too-broad pre-existing policy (for example an earlier `mc anonymous set download` on the whole bucket) is detected. The 'private' claim for health/ and everything else is only asserted. The dev checks cover listing (404 on /media/) but never request a non-media key anonymously, and /media/ proxying could not catch it since nginx pins the media/ prefix.
findings.evidence: server/src/storage.service.ts:22-32 (onModuleInit only calls ensureBucket); spec: 'At start-up the API sets a bucket policy that allows anonymous `s3:GetObject` on `media/*` only. Listing and every other prefix (for example the existing `health/` check) stay private.'
findings.fix:
Add to section 1 after the bucket-policy bullet (line 57):

"The policy is one Allow statement: Principal everyone, Action `s3:GetObject` only, Resource `arn:aws:s3:::${MINIO_BUCKET}/media/*`. It is written with PutBucketPolicy, which replaces any existing policy and never merges, so a broader policy from an earlier `mc anonymous set` is overwritten. After writing, the API reads it back with GetBucketPolicy and compares it to the expected statement by meaning (action, resource and principal sets, not the raw string, because MinIO may re-format the JSON). Start-up rules: (a) if the policy cannot be written or the read-back differs, the API logs the error once, still starts, and keeps media upload and the media admin endpoints disabled with 503 `STORAGE_UNAVAILABLE`; it never leaves a broader or unchecked policy in place; (b) if the key lacks the admin right to set policies, the same rule applies, and the deploy notes name the required right; (c) the check runs on every start, so drift is corrected at the next restart. This start-up step is separate from `ensureBucket`, so a policy failure cannot crash-loop the API."

Add to Testing (On dev), after the `GET /media/` bullet:

"From the dev host (MinIO ports are closed from outside), anonymous requests straight to MinIO: GET of an existing `health/` key returns 403; GET of `media/products/<id>/<file>.webp` returns 200; `?list-type=2` on the bucket, anonymous PUT and anonymous DELETE on a `media/` key all return 403. Read the stored policy with `mc admin` or GetBucketPolicy and confirm it equals the single statement above. Server unit test with a fake S3 client: a pre-existing broader policy is replaced, a differing read-back or a PutBucketPolicy failure leaves media endpoints returning 503 while the API still boots."
findings.verifyReason:
The code claim holds. server/src/storage.service.ts:22-32 only runs ensureBucket (HeadBucket, then CreateBucket on any error); nothing sets or reads a policy. The spec (section 1, line 57) says the API "sets a bucket policy" on media/* only, but gives no policy document, no failure rule, and no check that the stored policy is what was intended. S3 and MinIO PutBucketPolicy always replaces, so the "merge" worry is a non-issue, but the replace is silent and unchecked. A missing admin right would also make onModuleInit throw and crash-loop the API, since ensureBucket's catch does not guard the policy call.

Testing (lines 193-197) never requests a non-media key anonymously. Only /media/ and /media/products/ are probed through nginx, which pins the media/ prefix and so cannot reach health/. The reviewer's proposed test is partly wrong. "A media/ key under another bucket" is not meaningful, and its proposed rule to "refuse to start" contradicts "start with media disabled". Also, GetBucketPolicy read-back from MinIO may normalize the JSON (for example Principal becomes {"AWS":["*"]}), so an exact string match is fragile and should be a semantic comparison. Direct MinIO checks must run on the host, because ports 9000 and 9001 are closed from outside. No approved owner decision is reversed.

findings.title: A rejected duplicate upload deletes the files of the live photo because object keys are derived only from the hash
findings.section: 2. Upload, processing and access control (Order of work)
findings.problem: Upload writes the WebP files first, then inserts the row; 'if the transaction fails, delete the files again'. Keys are media/products/{productId}/{hash16}-{width}.webp, identical for an identical photo. When the same photo is uploaded twice, the second request overwrites the same keys, the (productId, hash) unique constraint then rejects the insert with 409, and the cleanup deletes the files that the first (live, published) photo points to. Shoppers then get broken images (falling back to the drawing) and the audit log still says the photo exists. The same happens when two simultaneous uploads of one file race.
findings.evidence: spec: 'Upload: write the WebP files to MinIO; then in one transaction insert the row ... if the transaction fails, delete the files again.' and 'The same photo uploaded twice to one product is refused' with key 'media/products/{productId}/{hash16}-{width}.webp'.
findings.fix: Replace the Upload bullet (line 105) with: "Upload: take a per-product lock first (`pg_advisory_xact_lock` on the productId inside the transaction, or the equivalent row lock on the product). Under the lock: compute the hash, and if a row with the same (productId, hash) exists refuse with 409 CONFLICT 'Foto ini sudah ada di produk ini' before writing anything. Otherwise write only keys that do not already exist (HeadObject first, or PutObject with If-None-Match: *) and remember which keys this request created. Then insert the row at the first free position and write the audit entry in the same transaction. If the transaction fails, delete only the keys this request created, never keys that already existed and never keys of a photo whose row exists. The lock also serialises two simultaneous uploads on the same product, so the (productId, position) unique key stays as a safety net that still returns 409 'Foto lain sedang diunggah. Coba lagi.' Test: uploading the same file twice leaves all three files in the bucket, the second request returns 409 CONFLICT, and the first photo's three URLs still answer 200. A second test fires two simultaneous uploads of one file: exactly one succeeds, one gets 409, and all three files still exist."
findings.verifyReason: Spec line 55 keys files as media/products/{productId}/{hash16}-{width}.webp, so the same photo always maps to the same keys. Line 101 says a repeat is refused, and line 105 writes files first, then inserts the row, and deletes the files if the transaction fails. A repeat or racing upload therefore overwrites the live photo's keys, the (productId, hash) unique constraint rejects the insert with 409, and the cleanup deletes the live photo's files. The spec has no pre-check and no rule limiting cleanup to keys the request created. This contradicts the spec's goal that a failure never leaves a half-finished photo. The reviewer's fix is directionally right but incomplete. A check-then-write with a post-failure re-check still races: request B can delete files that request A has written but not yet committed. The fix needs per-product serialisation, or cleanup restricted to keys this request created.

findings.title: Image processing has no concurrency, memory or CPU bound, so one staff session can starve the API that also serves checkout
findings.problem: Each upload decodes up to 40 MP (about 160 MB raw RGBA) plus up to three resize encodes, from a 10 MB in-memory buffer, in the same Node process and container as checkout and payments. No limit on simultaneous uploads, sharp thread/cache settings, container memory limit, or rate limit per staff is specified. A compromised or careless staff account, or a few parallel uploads, can OOM-kill the API during a payment webhook. limitInputPixels is also described as stopping decompression bombs but it only bounds pixel count; the spec does not say how animated WebP/APNG (many frames) or truncated files are handled.
findings.evidence: spec: 'at most 40 megapixels (`limitInputPixels`), which also blocks decompression bombs'; docker-compose.yml:3-10 (api service has no mem_limit or deploy resources).
findings.fix:
Add to section 2, after the Processing bullets (line 99):

"Resource bounds (image work shares the API process with checkout and payment webhooks):
- '40 megapixels' means 40,000,000 pixels. sharp is opened with `{ limitInputPixels: 40_000_000, failOn: 'error' }` and `animated` left false, so only the first frame is read. A truncated or corrupt file fails decoding and returns 422 `VALIDATION` ('Foto tidak dapat dibaca. Coba file lain.'). No other animated or multi-frame handling is added; GIF stays refused.
- Image work runs behind an in-process limiter of 2 concurrent jobs. A request that cannot start within 10 s returns 503 `STORAGE_UNAVAILABLE` with a `Retry-After` header. Multer buffers are released as soon as the job ends.
- sharp is configured at startup with `sharp.cache(false)` and `sharp.concurrency(2)`.
- Uploads are limited to 20 per staff member per 10 minutes (429 `RATE_LIMITED`, 'Terlalu banyak unggahan. Coba lagi nanti.'). The limit is audited on trip or logged.
- docker-compose.yml gives the `api` service a memory limit. The value is set in the plan from a measured peak RSS and is at least 1 GB (two 40 MP decodes are about 320 MB plus the 10 MB buffers and the Node baseline).
- Test: ten parallel 40 MP uploads keep peak RSS below the limit, none hangs, and a checkout request issued during the burst still returns within its normal time."
findings.verifyReason: The spec (lines 90-99) specifies only a 10 MB in-memory multer limit and `limitInputPixels` at 40 MP. It says nothing about simultaneous uploads, sharp concurrency or cache, a per-staff rate limit, or truncated and multi-frame files. docker-compose.yml's `api` service has no `mem_limit` or `deploy.resources`, and it is the same container that serves checkout and payment webhooks. A 40 MP decode is about 160 MB of raw RGBA, so a few parallel uploads can reach OOM. The fix does not reverse any approved owner decision: 10 MB, JPEG/PNG/WebP, 6 photos, 480/960/1600 WebP and the roles are all untouched. Two details are refined. First, sharp already reads only the first frame of an animated file unless `animated: true` is set, so the spec should state the intended behaviour explicitly rather than invent a new rejection. Second, the 1 GB floor and the limiter numbers are plan-level values to be measured, not fixed in the spec.

findings.title: /media proxy is a prefix match that forwards the query string, maps only 403, and leaks MinIO identity headers
findings.problem: A prefix `location /media/` with proxy_pass to http://host.docker.internal:9000/${MINIO_BUCKET}/media/ forwards the raw query string (S3 sub-resource and response-override parameters) to MinIO, accepts any key shape under the prefix, and lets encoded or odd paths (/media/%2e%2e/, //, backslash, %2f) reach the backend; only the bucket policy limits damage. Error mapping covers 403 only: a MinIO 400, 5xx or a connection failure would return MinIO's XML error body (bucket name, request id) or nginx's default 502 page. Only 'x-amz-*' headers are hidden, but MinIO also sends Server, x-minio-*, Accept-Ranges, ETag and Strict-Transport-Security headers that identify the backend. The spec also does not say what the 403 for non-GET methods is, or that the Cache-Control immutable header must not apply to error responses.
findings.evidence: spec: '/media/ answers with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` ..., hides MinIO's `x-amz-*` headers, refuses other methods, and turns MinIO's 403 into a plain 404 (`proxy_intercept_errors`).' web/nginx.conf has no /media location yet; existing /v1/ block shows the prefix style used.
findings.fix:
Replace the first and third bullets of "3. Serving and caching" with:

- `web/nginx.conf` gains an allowlist location `location ~ ^/media/(products/[A-Za-z0-9_-]+/[0-9a-f]{16}-(480|960|1600)\.webp)$ { ... }`. It uses `limit_except GET HEAD { deny all; }` plus `error_page 403 =405` for the method case, so any other method gets 405. It sets `rewrite ^ /${MINIO_BUCKET}/media/$1 break;` and then `proxy_pass http://host.docker.internal:9000;` (no URI part, no variables, so no `resolver` is needed and the query string is not forwarded: add `proxy_set_header` and `proxy_pass_request_body off;` and also `set $args "";` before the rewrite). Any other `/media/...` path, including `/media/`, `/media/products/`, odd encodings and any key not matching the pattern, is answered by `location /media/ { return 404; }` from nginx without contacting MinIO.
- In the media location, `proxy_hide_header` removes `Server`, `x-amz-*` (`x-amz-request-id`, `x-amz-id-2`, `x-amz-version-id`), `x-minio-*`, `Strict-Transport-Security`, `Accept-Ranges` and `ETag` if not needed. `proxy_intercept_errors on;` with `error_page 400 401 403 404 500 502 503 504 = @media_404;` and `location @media_404 { internal; default_type text/plain; return 404 ""; }`, so every upstream error and connection failure becomes an empty 404 with no MinIO body or headers. `proxy_next_upstream off;`.
- The success headers `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` are added with `add_header` WITHOUT the `always` parameter, so they are never sent on error responses. Error responses are `Cache-Control: no-store`, set explicitly inside `@media_404`. `proxy_hide_header Content-Type; add_header Content-Type image/webp;` (or `default_type image/webp` with the upstream header hidden) so the type is always `image/webp`.

Add to the dev checks: `/media/%2e%2e/health`, `/media/..%2fhealth`, `/media//products/B01/x.webp`, `/media/products/B01/x.webp?response-content-type=text/html` and `/media/products/B01/1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b-960.webp?response-content-type=text/html` (a real file, which must be served without the override) each return the expected result. The first four return 404, and the fifth returns 200 as `image/webp`. All of them show no `Server: MinIO`, `x-amz-*` or `x-minio-*` header and no XML body. `POST /media/products/B01/1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b-960.webp` returns 405. Stopping MinIO returns an empty 404, not nginx's 502 page. `nginx -t` runs in the web image build for the rendered template.
findings.verifyReason: Spec line 116 says only "refuses other methods", maps MinIO's 403 to 404, and hides `x-amz-*`. Line 114 describes a prefix `/media/` proxy to a fixed bucket URI. The existing web/nginx.conf uses prefix locations (`/v1/`, `/assets/`) and has no `/media` block or `error_page`. Four points hold. (1) With a prefix location and a `proxy_pass` URI, nginx appends the query string, so S3 response-override parameters reach MinIO. (2) Mapping only 403 leaves 400, 5xx and connection failures returning MinIO's XML error body (bucket name, request id) or nginx's default 502 page. (3) `Server`, `x-minio-*` and similar headers are not hidden. (4) The method-refusal status is unspecified. The impact is bounded by the anonymous `media/*` GetObject policy, so severity is moderate, not major. The reviewer's fix needs three corrections. A regex location cannot use `proxy_pass` with a URI part. Variables in `proxy_pass` need a `resolver`, and `host.docker.internal` is resolved through `extra_hosts`. So the proxy target must be built with `rewrite ... break;` and `proxy_pass` written without a URI, or with `$request_uri` handled carefully. Second, `add_header` without `always` already skips error responses, so the fix should say "no `always`" and not "always only for 200/206". Third, nginx decodes and normalises `%2e%2e` before matching, so the regex allowlist is enough for those cases. The checks should still be kept as regression tests. The allowlist matches the approved name format in the item 1 decisions (`media/products/{productId}/{hash16}-{width}.webp`), so it does not reverse any owner decision.

findings.title: Audit entries are underspecified for attribution, and the sample scripts are outside the audit and ALCOA+ rules
findings.section: 2. Upload ... (Audit codes) / 5. Demo photos, credits and removal
findings.problem: The audit table is actor (a display string), at, code, action, object, before, after. The spec lists only code names. It does not define the before/after content, so 'original' evidence is thin: originals are discarded and neither the uploaded file's name, size, source hash nor the resulting image id appear anywhere. VARIANT_IMAGE_LINKED has a sku as its natural object but the spec says every object is productId. Actor is 'name (Role)', not the staff id used for createdBy, so a renamed user breaks attribution. `media:remove-samples` is said to write audit entries but has no actor (it runs in a container shell, not under a staff session) and `media:seed` writes rows with createdBy 'seed' and no audit entry at all; both change data shown to customers.
findings.evidence: server/prisma/schema.prisma:122-131 `model AuditRecord { at, actor, code, action, object, before Json?, after Json? }`; server/src/commerce/admin.service.ts:167-169 `return `${user.name} (${ROLE_LABEL[user.role]})``; spec: 'Audit codes, each with actor, time, object (`productId`), before and after' and '`npm run media:remove-samples` deletes every sample photo (rows and files) with audit entries.'
findings.fix:
Append to the end of the "Audit codes" paragraph in section 2:

"Payloads (all JSON). The object is the productId for every media code, except VARIANT_IMAGE_LINKED, whose object is the variant SKU. Every media audit entry carries `actorId` (the staff id, or `cli` for scripts) inside `after` (or inside `before` when `after` is null), so attribution survives a staff rename. The existing `name (Role)` actor string format stays unchanged.
- PRODUCT_IMAGE_ADDED: before = null; after = { imageId, position, alt, hash, sizes, width, height, uploadedBytes, uploadedFilename (as sent, truncated to 120 characters, stored only here and never used in any storage key), actorId }.
- PRODUCT_IMAGE_REMOVED: before = the full removed row, including hash, position, alt and source; after = { actorId }.
- PRODUCT_IMAGE_REORDERED: before and after = the ordered lists of image ids.
- PRODUCT_IMAGE_ALT_CHANGED: before and after = { imageId, alt }.
- VARIANT_IMAGE_LINKED: before and after = { imageId or null }.
The audit entry is always written in the same transaction as the row change."

Append to section 5, after the media:seed and media:remove-samples bullets:

"Both scripts write one audit entry per photo, in the same transaction as the row change. The actor is `CLI:{operator}`, where operator comes from `--operator <name>` and falls back to the OS user name. media:remove-samples refuses to run without an explicit `--operator`. media:seed uses codes PRODUCT_IMAGE_ADDED or PRODUCT_IMAGE_REMOVED as appropriate, and its `createdBy: \"seed\"` value stays unchanged. If a script run changes nothing, it writes no audit entries."
findings.verifyReason: The gaps are real. The AuditRecord model (schema.prisma:122-131) has only at, actor (a string), code, action, object, before and after. Spec line 110 lists code names and says only "actor, time, object (productId), before and after", so the payloads are undefined. Line 22 (constraint 7) requires before and after for every admin mutation. Line 155 says media:remove-samples writes "audit entries" but names no actor, and the script runs from a container shell with no staff session. media:seed (line 154) writes rows with createdBy "seed" and no audit entry, even though customers see those rows. The spec states the actor and object (productId) conventions but never says that the actor string carries no staff id, or that variant links use productId rather than the SKU. Two parts of the proposed fix go too far. First, changing the global actor format ("name (Role) [id]") would alter every existing audit entry, which is out of scope. Put the staff id in the payload for media events instead. Second, a mandatory --operator flag would break the unattended deploy step (docs line 205 runs media:seed in the deploy sequence). Use an optional flag with a fallback, and require the flag only for remove-samples, which is destructive.

findings.title: Spec's 409/413/415/422 error table cannot be produced: ApiExceptionFilter turns multer, Prisma unique-key and sharp errors into 500 or generic VALIDATION
findings.section: 2. Upload, processing and access control / Error messages
findings.problem: The spec relies on the (productId, position) and (productId, hash) unique keys to produce 409s, and on Multer's 10 MB limit to produce 413 TOO_LARGE. The existing filter only emits a custom code when the HttpException body carries `code`. Multer's limit error is rethrown by Nest's FileInterceptor as a plain PayloadTooLargeException (no `code`), so the client gets 413 with code VALIDATION and an English message. A Prisma P2002 (unique violation) is not an HttpException, not RangeError/TypeError and not P2028/P2034, so it falls through to 500 INTERNAL 'Terjadi kesalahan pada server.'. Sharp's 'Input image exceeds pixel limit' and corrupt-file errors are plain Errors, also 500. The spec does not say where these are mapped, and the two P2002 cases (position vs hash) must be told apart by meta.target.
findings.evidence: server/src/api-exception.filter.ts:22-31 (`if (typeof body === "object" && body && "code" in body)` else `code: status === 404 ? "NOT_FOUND" : "VALIDATION"`); :34-44 (only P2028/P2034 mapped, everything else 500). Spec lines 105 ('the unique key makes the second fail with 409') and 163 (Over 10 MB -> 413 TOO_LARGE).
findings.fix:
Add to section 2 after the "Checks on upload" list:

"Error mapping. The global ApiExceptionFilter only keeps a custom code when the HttpException body carries `code`, and it maps unknown errors to 500. So every error in the table above must be raised as an HttpException with `{ code, message }`. This work stays in the media upload path, and the global filter is not changed.
1. MediaService wraps its transaction and processing steps and rethrows:
   - Prisma P2002 with `meta.target` containing `position` -> 409 `CONFLICT` "Foto lain sedang diunggah. Coba lagi."
   - Prisma P2002 with `meta.target` containing `hash` -> 409 `CONFLICT` "Foto ini sudah ada di produk ini."
   - Any other P2002 is not mapped and stays 500, because it is a bug.
   - A sharp error on decode (corrupt file) -> 422 `VALIDATION` "File foto rusak atau tidak bisa dibaca."
   - sharp's "exceeds pixel limit" error, raised by `limitInputPixels` of 40 MP -> 422 `VALIDATION` "Foto terlalu besar untuk diproses (maks. 40 megapiksel)."
   - S3/MinIO client errors (connection refused, timeout) -> 503 `STORAGE_UNAVAILABLE` "Penyimpanan foto sedang tidak tersedia. Coba lagi sebentar." Add this row to the error table.
2. Multer limits. Nest's FileInterceptor already converts `LIMIT_FILE_SIZE` into a plain PayloadTooLargeException (413) and unexpected-field or missing-file cases into BadRequestException (400), all without `code`. Add a small exception filter, applied with @UseFilters on the upload route only, that catches PayloadTooLargeException and rethrows 413 `{ code: "TOO_LARGE", message: "Ukuran file maksimal 10 MB." }`. It also catches BadRequestException from the interceptor, and a missing `file` field, and returns 422 `{ code: "VALIDATION", message: "File foto wajib dilampirkan." }`.
3. Add one unit test per mapping above: the two P2002 targets, corrupt file, pixel limit, storage unavailable, Multer size limit and missing file. Each test asserts both the HTTP status and the `error.code` in the response body."
findings.verifyReason: Checked server/src/api-exception.filter.ts. An HttpException without `code` in its body gets code VALIDATION, or NOT_FOUND for 404, with the original English message. Nest's FileInterceptor rethrows Multer's LIMIT_FILE_SIZE as a plain PayloadTooLargeException, so a client would get 413 with VALIDATION, not TOO_LARGE. A Prisma P2002 is not an HttpException and not P2028/P2034, and it is not a RangeError or TypeError. It therefore falls to the final branch and returns 500 INTERNAL. The same applies to plain Errors from sharp (pixel limit, corrupt input) and to S3 client errors. The spec's lines 105 and 161-171 promise 409, 413, 415 and 422 codes but never say where they are mapped, and the two P2002 cases must be told apart by meta.target. Nothing in the approved owner decisions is reversed by the fix.

findings.title: Closing the position gap on delete (and in remove-samples) can violate the non-deferrable unique key and leave no photo at position 0
findings.problem: Reorder is protected with the +100 two-step, but Delete says only 'close the gap in positions'. Postgres checks a non-deferrable unique index per row during an UPDATE, so a single `position = position - 1` over rows 1,2,3 can collide depending on physical row order (the exact problem the reorder step was designed around). Separately, media:remove-samples deletes only source:'sample' rows: if a client has uploaded photos next to samples (possible after seed), the remaining uploads keep positions such as 1,2 with nothing at 0, breaking the rule 'position 0 is the main photo' and the catalogue's main-photo choice. The spec does not say remove-samples renumbers.
findings.evidence: Spec line 39 (`@@unique([productId, position])`), line 106 (Reorder uses +100 step), line 107 (Delete: 'close the gap in positions'), line 155 (remove-samples 'deletes every sample photo'). server/prisma/schema.prisma has no deferrable constraint support (Prisma cannot declare one).
findings.fix:
Section 2, Delete (line 107). Replace "close the gap in positions" with: "renumber the remaining photos of the product with the same routine as reorder, never with a single decrement UPDATE: first set every remaining photo of the product to position + 100, then write the final positions 0..n-1 in the existing order. This runs inside the same transaction as the row delete and the audit entry. The renumber routine is one shared service method used by reorder, delete and remove-samples."

Section 3, schema (line 40). Add: "The 0-5 range is enforced in the service layer, not by a DB CHECK constraint, so the temporary +100 positions used during renumbering are allowed. Only the unique key applies at the database level."

Section 5, `media:remove-samples` (line 155). Append: "It removes the sample rows of each product through the same delete service method as staff delete, so the audit entries and the variant-link clearing (`onDelete: SetNull`) behave identically. After the deletes it renumbers that product's remaining photos with the shared two-step routine, so position 0 is always the main photo. Products left with no photos fall back to the drawing."

Tests (around line 189). Add: "(a) Delete the middle photo of three. The remaining positions are 0,1 and no unique-key violation occurs. (b) Delete the photo at position 0. The former position 1 becomes the main photo. (c) `remove-samples` on a product with 2 sample photos plus 2 uploads. The uploads end at positions 0,1, one audit entry is written per removed sample, and any variant link to a removed photo is cleared."
findings.verifyReason: The spec has the gap on both counts. Line 40 declares `@@unique([productId, position])`. Prisma cannot declare it as deferrable, so Postgres checks it row by row during an UPDATE. Line 106 uses the +100 two-step for reorder precisely because of this. Line 107 says Delete only "close the gap in positions" and names no technique. A bare `position = position - 1` over positions 1,2,3 can collide, depending on the order the rows are physically updated. Line 155 says `media:remove-samples` "deletes every sample photo (rows and files) with audit entries" and says nothing about renumbering. Line 189 says it "touches only source: sample rows". The seed skips products that already have photos, but staff uploads can sit next to samples, with uploads taking the first free position after them. Removing the samples would then leave uploads at positions such as 1 and 2 with nothing at 0. That breaks the rule on line 40 that 0 is the main photo, and the catalogue (line 70) orders by position. The handoff's "Item 1 decisions" do not fix a delete or renumber method, so the fix reverses no approved decision. One caveat: the +100 step needs the 0-5 range to be enforced in application code, not as a DB CHECK constraint. Line 40 states the range but not how it is enforced.

findings.title: media:seed / media:remove-samples cannot run in the API image as the Dockerfile stands; seed lifecycle and LAUNCH_CHECKLIST are underspecified
findings.section: 5. Demo photos, credits and removal / Rollout on dev
findings.problem: The spec adds only `COPY seed ./seed` and runs `docker compose exec api npm run media:seed`. The image copies only package.json, prisma, tsconfig*, vitest.config.ts and src; server/scripts/ is NOT copied (the existing `totp:setup` script lives there and is run locally only), and the image holds compiled dist/ with no tsx/ts-node. "- The two scripts are TypeScript under `server/src/media/cli/` (`seed.ts`, `remove-samples.ts`). `npm run build` compiles them, and they run as `node dist/media/cli/seed.js` and `node dist/media/cli/remove-samples.js`. `server/package.json` gets `\"media:seed\": \"node dist/media/cli/seed.js\"` and `\"media:remove-samples\": \"node dist/media/cli/remove-samples.js\"`. It runs `npm test` and `npm run build` in one RUN, and CMD is `node dist/main.js`. server/package.json has no media:* scripts, and totp:setup is `node scripts/totp-setup.mjs`, a folder the image does not copy. findings.title: Dependency details missing: @types/multer is not installed and tsconfig `types: ["node"]` hides it; sharp version and HEIC/orientation behaviour not pinned down
findings.problem: Multer itself is available (it is a dependency of @nestjs/platform-express 10.4.15), so no `multer` package is needed, but nothing provides the typings: server devDependencies have only @types/node, and tsconfig.json restricts global types to `["node"]`, so `Express.Multer.File` will not compile even after adding @types/multer unless the types list or an explicit `import type` is added. The spec says only 'exact version pinned' for sharp without naming one; the image has no lockfile (Dockerfile copies package.json only and runs `npm install`), so an exact version in package.json is the only pin. Further: the type check is described as `sharp().metadata().format` accepting jpeg/png/webp and refusing HEIC with its own message, but the prebuilt sharp/libvips binaries decode AVIF only, not HEVC-based HEIC, so metadata() on an iPhone HEIC may throw rather than return format 'heif', making the 'HEIC' message path untestable as written. Finally `metadata().width/height` are the pre-rotation values, so for portrait phone photos (EXIF orientation 5-8) the 'shorter side >= 480' check and the 'widths not larger than the photo' rule use swapped dimensions unless orientation is applied first.
findings.evidence: server/package.json:14-28 (dependencies: @nestjs/platform-express 10.4.15, no sharp, no @types/multer; devDependencies: @types/node, prisma, typescript, vitest). server/tsconfig.json:14 (`"types": ["node"]`). server/Dockerfile:9-10 (`COPY package.json ./` then `RUN npm install`, no package-lock). Spec lines 91 and 96-98.
findings.fix:
In section 2 add a "Dependencies" paragraph: "`sharp` 0.33.5 (exact version, in `dependencies`; prebuilt linux-x64 glibc binary, runs on `node:22-bookworm-slim`). `@types/multer` 1.4.12 (exact, in `devDependencies`), and `server/tsconfig.json` `types` becomes `[\"node\", \"multer\"]` so `Express.Multer.File` compiles. Multer itself arrives through `@nestjs/platform-express` and is not added directly. findings.title: nginx/compose plan: MINIO_BUCKET is not available to the web service, and proxy_hide_header / proxy_intercept_errors are specified in ways that do not work
findings.problem: (1) `${MINIO_BUCKET}` lives only in server/.env, which is the api service's env_file. The root docker-compose.yml web service has no env_file/environment, and compose `${VAR}` interpolation reads the shell or the root .env, whose documented contents are POSTGRES_* and the SSH key, not MINIO_*. 'Passes MINIO_BUCKET to it' therefore yields an empty value; envsubst then writes `proxy_pass http://host.docker.internal:9000//media/`, so every image 404s while the API still works. (2) nginx's `proxy_hide_header` takes exact header names; it has no wildcard, so 'hides MinIO's x-amz-* headers' is not implementable as worded (MinIO sends x-amz-request-id, x-amz-id-2, x-amz-version-id and others). (3) `proxy_intercept_errors on` only makes nginx consult `error_page`; without an `error_page 403 =404 ...` directive MinIO's 403 (what anonymous GET returns for a missing key when ListBucket is not granted) passes through unchanged. (4) The image build only does `COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf`; moving to /etc/nginx/templates also needs the Dockerfile COPY changed and the old conf.d copy removed, and the spec does not list web/Dockerfile as a changed file. (5) The API's PutBucketPolicy needs the MinIO access key to have s3:PutBucketPolicy, which the current key is only known to use for HeadBucket/CreateBucket/PutObject/GetObject.
findings.evidence: docker-compose.yml:11-17 (web service: build, ports, depends_on only); server/.env.example:7 (`MINIO_BUCKET=tian-media`); architecture.md:49 (root .env holds POSTGRES_DB_NAME/POSTGRES_USER/POSTGRES_PORT); web/Dockerfile:12 (`COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf`); server/src/storage.service.ts:1,26-32 (only Head/CreateBucket/Put/Get used, no policy call). Spec lines 114-116.
findings.fix:
Replace spec lines 114-116 (section 3, first three bullets) with:

- `web/nginx.conf` gains a `/media/` location that proxies GET and HEAD to `http://host.docker.internal:9000/${MINIO_BUCKET}/media/`, the same route the API already uses. `docker-compose.yml` gives the web service `extra_hosts: ["host.docker.internal:host-gateway"]` (as the API service has) and `environment: { MINIO_BUCKET: "${MINIO_BUCKET:-tian-media}" }`. Compose interpolation reads the root `.env`, not `server/.env`, so `MINIO_BUCKET=tian-media` is added to the root `.env.example` and to the root `.env` on dev.
- `web/Dockerfile` changes `COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf` to `COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/templates/default.conf.template`; the conf.d copy is removed. `web/Dockerfile` is listed among the changed files. The official image's start-up `envsubst` fills `${MINIO_BUCKET}`; it only replaces variables that exist in the environment, so nginx's own `$uri` and friends are untouched.
- `/media/` answers with `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, and refuses methods other than GET and HEAD. `proxy_hide_header` has no wildcard, so it is listed one header per line: `x-amz-request-id`, `x-amz-id-2`, `x-amz-version-id`, `Server`, `Set-Cookie`, plus any other `x-amz-*` header seen in `curl -I` against dev. MinIO's 403 is turned into a plain 404 with `proxy_intercept_errors on; error_page 403 404 = @media_missing;` and `location @media_missing { return 404; }`.

Add to section 1, after the bucket-policy sentence (line 57): "The MinIO access key used by the API must be allowed `s3:PutBucketPolicy` and `s3:DeleteObject` on the bucket. If the policy call fails at start-up, the API logs a warning and continues; the owner then sets the policy once with `mc anonymous set download <alias>/<bucket>/media`. The dev check includes an anonymous GET of one `/media/...` file (200, with the cache headers) and an anonymous GET of a missing key (404, not 403)."
findings.verifyReason: Checked against the spec and code. (1) docker-compose.yml web service has no env_file or environment, and the spec only says it "passes MINIO_BUCKET". MINIO_BUCKET is in server/.env, which only feeds the api service, so envsubst would yield an empty value. (2) nginx proxy_hide_header takes exact names with no wildcard, so "hides x-amz-*" is not implementable as worded. (3) proxy_intercept_errors only has effect with an error_page directive, and the spec (line 116) names none. (4) web/Dockerfile line 11 copies to conf.d/default.conf. Spec line 115 moves the file to the templates dir but never lists web/Dockerfile as changed (grep finds no Dockerfile mention for web). (5) storage.service.ts uses only Head/CreateBucket/Put/Get, so PutBucketPolicy permission on the current key is unverified. Point 5 is an unverified assumption, not a proven defect, so the fix makes the policy call non-fatal. Nothing here reverses an owner decision. It corrects the implementation mechanics.
